summary: Describes a Diameter application that gives per-endpoint control of Network Address Translators and Network Address and Port Translators, deployed to cope with IPv4 address depletion. It defines the framework, messages, and procedures for that control. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A NAT is like a receptionist sharing one phone number among many people. This memo lets a manager tell the receptionist how to treat each person.

subtitle: A Diameter application that lets a provider's AAA systems control address translators one subscriber at a time.

tldr.problem: Providers put NAT and NAPT devices in their networks because public IPv4 addresses ran short, but a NAT with no idea who each endpoint is cannot offer per-subscriber limits, static bindings, address pools or per-subscriber reporting.
tldr.mechanism: The Diameter Network address and port translation Control Application (DNCA) lets a NAT controller open one Diameter session per endpoint with a NAT device. Over it, NAT-Control-Request and NAT-Control-Answer messages install, update, remove and query bindings, and Diameter accounting reports them.
tldr.outcome: A provider can fit NAT control into its existing Diameter AAA environment, capping bindings per endpoint, pre-allocating specific bindings, choosing address pools and collecting per-endpoint accounting. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 6736 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines how a Diameter-based NAT controller manages NAT44 and NAT64 devices per endpoint. It builds on the Diameter base protocol in RFC 6733.

sections.title: Why Control a NAT Per Endpoint
sections.content:
Internet service providers deploy Network Address Translators (NATs) and Network Address and Port Translators (NAPTs), described in RFC 3022, in large part because public IPv4 addresses are running out. RFC 6736 defines a Diameter application, the Diameter Network address and port translation Control Application (DNCA), that lets a provider control those devices from its existing Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) environment. It covers IPv4-to-IPv4 translation (NAT44) and stateful IPv6-to-IPv4 translation (NAT64).

The RFC lists six capabilities: limit the number of bindings an endpoint may have; allocate specific bindings, either fully predefined or with the external address chosen by the NAT; define the external address pools to use; generate reports and accounting records; query bindings on demand; and identify an endpoint consistently across the NAT, the AAA server and the network access server (NAS).

The main reason for a per-endpoint binding limit is protection against denial of service. If endpoints share one public address and one of them uses up all the bindings, the others lose service.

With these capabilities DNCA qualifies as a Middlebox Communications (MIDCOM) protocol, and the RFC says it adds the ability to tie control operations to an endpoint that represents a user or subscriber.
sections.plainLanguage: When many families share one phone line, one noisy family could hog it. This memo lets the phone company set a fair limit for each family and keep track of who uses what.

sections.title: The Deployment Framework
sections.content:
DNCA runs between two Diameter peers: one inside the NAT device and one inside a NAT controller. The controller always acts as the control-requesting side. It starts, updates and ends sessions. A session is created when the controller learns of a new endpoint that needs NAT service, for example because it sees authentication or accounting requests for it.

An endpoint is a managed entity tied to a subscriber, a user or a group of users. It is represented by a single access session on a NAS, and the RFC assumes a one-to-one-to-one relationship between the endpoint, its access session and its DNCA session.

Two deployments are described. In the integrated deployment the NAS is the NAT controller. It hides the NAT device from the AAA server and merges the NAT device's accounting data with its own into a single stream. In the autonomous deployment the AAA system is the NAT controller, so the AAA server sees two accounting streams for one endpoint: one from the NAS and one from the NAT device.

DNCA supports n controllers and m NAT devices, but for any given endpoint only a single NAT controller MUST be active at a time. If an operator also configures the NAT through other means such as a command line, SNMP or PCP, the operator MUST make sure the configurations do not conflict, and the NAT device MUST let the operator set a policy for resolving conflicts.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a boss (the controller) giving orders to a worker (the NAT device) about one customer at a time. Only one boss at a time may give orders about a given customer, so the worker never gets mixed signals.

sections.title: Sessions: Establish, Update, Query, End
sections.content:
Session setup starts with a NAT-Control-Request (NCR) whose NC-Request-Type is INITIAL_REQUEST. The NAT device creates session state only if it can comply, and replies with a NAT-Control-Answer (NCA) carrying DIAMETER_SUCCESS. The first request may carry a list of bindings to pre-allocate, a maximum number of bindings, external address pools, or a reference to a predefined binding template on the NAT device. If a request includes both explicit values and a template, the explicit Max-NAT-Bindings and NAT-Control-Definition values override the template.

An NCR is atomic: either every requested action succeeds or the whole request fails and no requested binding is established. Typical failures are answered with SESSION_EXISTS, INSUFFICIENT_CLASSIFIERS, UNKNOWN_BINDING_TEMPLATE_NAME, BINDING_FAILURE, MAX_BINDINGS_SET_FAILURE and RESOURCE_FAILURE.

An UPDATE_REQUEST changes an existing session, for example the allowed number of bindings or the set of predefined bindings. If a new maximum is lower than the number of bindings already allocated, the NAT device SHOULD NOT tear bindings down at once but refuse new ones until the count falls below the limit. A QUERY_REQUEST either lists the bindings for a given Session-Id, or finds the sessions that use a given internal address or external address and port pair.

Termination is also started by the controller, with a Session-Termination-Request (STR). The NAT device MAY send an accounting stop record, MUST remove all bindings of the session, and answers with a Session-Termination-Answer (STA). The NAT device can instead send an Abort-Session-Request (ASR) when it cannot keep a session because of resource limits.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss says 'start looking after this customer', 'change the rules for this customer', 'tell me what this customer has', or 'stop'. The worker either does the whole job or none of it, so nothing is left half done.

sections.title: Commands and AVPs
sections.content:
DNCA defines one request/answer pair. NAT-Control-Request (NCR) and NAT-Control-Answer (NCA) use command code 330, and the application identifier is 12. Nodes advertise support by including 12 in the Auth-Application-Id of Capabilities-Exchange messages. The endpoint is identified by AVPs such as Framed-IP-Address, Framed-IPv6-Prefix, User-Name and Calling-Station-ID.

New AVPs use codes 595 to 607. The key ones are:

  • NAT-Control-Install and NAT-Control-Remove: grouped AVPs that add or remove bindings.
  • NAT-Control-Definition: describes one binding, with an internal address, and optionally a protocol, a direction and an external address. If both internal and external addresses are given, it is a predefined binding.
  • Max-NAT-Bindings: the cap on bindings for the endpoint.
  • NAT-Control-Binding-Template: names a policy template predefined on the NAT device. Its contents are outside the scope of the RFC.
  • NAT-External-Port-Style: its one defined value, FOLLOW_INTERNAL_PORT_STYLE, makes external ports follow the oddity and sequence of the internal ports, which supports protocols such as RTP and RTCP.

Six new Result-Code values are defined: 4014 for the transient RESOURCE_FAILURE, and 5042 to 5047 for the permanent failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages are like forms with labelled boxes: who the customer is, how many connections they may have, and which public address to use. Each box has a number so both sides read the form the same way.

sections.title: Session State and Failures
sections.content:
The RFC gives state tables, which MUST be observed by all implementations, for both peers. The controller side moves through Idle, Pending, Open and Discon. It sends an initial NCR from Idle, goes Open on a successful NCA, and sends an STR when the access session ends. Any event not listed in a table is an error condition.

The RFC does not specify what happens when the controller and the NAT device get out of sync or lose state, but it gives examples. If the controller loses state and sends an initial request that matches an existing session, the NAT device returns the existing Session-Id in a Duplicate-Session-Id AVP and the controller MAY send an STR for the old session. If the controller becomes unreachable, the NAT device MUST clean up bindings and state after a configurable grace period, which can be zero or more.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side keeps a checklist of what step a customer is on: not started, waiting, active, or ending. If a side forgets the list, the rules say how to find the old entry and tidy up.

sections.title: Accounting and Reporting
sections.content:
DNCA reuses Diameter session-based accounting. The NAT device sends Accounting-Request (ACR) messages of type Start, Interim and Stop to the controller. It sends a Start on receiving an initial NCR (or when the first binding is created), Interims when bindings change or at the interval set in Acct-Interim-Interval, and a Stop on receiving an STR.

Each ACR carries Current-NAT-Bindings (the number of active bindings) and zero or more NAT-Control-Record AVPs. A record pairs a NAT-Control-Definition with a NAT-Control-Binding-Status of Created (1), Active (2) or Removed (3), and an optional Event-Timestamp. Correlating the multiple bindings an endpoint uses over time is left to a post processor.
sections.plainLanguage: The worker sends the boss regular receipts listing which connections were opened, are still open, or were closed for each customer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because DNCA lets a non-local entity change NAT behavior, the RFC stresses authentication, authorization, integrity and confidentiality. An attacker who could spoof a controller might, for instance, set an endpoint's maximum bindings to zero, provision bindings that clash with addresses used elsewhere, or terminate sessions. If DNCA traffic crosses untrusted networks, messages SHOULD be secured with IPsec or TLS, peers SHOULD authenticate each other, and the Session-Id SHOULD be hard to guess to limit replay.

The RFC also warns that any NAT control mechanism can be misused, for example for censorship, redirecting traffic through a snooping relay, or anti-competitive practices. These protections do not prevent abuse by an authorized controller, and preventing it is outside the scope of the specification. If a session ends unexpectedly and the grace period is zero, the endpoint immediately loses connectivity through the NAT device.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger could order the worker around, they could cut off a customer or send their calls the wrong way. So the boss and worker must prove who they are and keep their messages secret.

messages.label: NCR (INITIAL_REQUEST)
messages.note: Asks the NAT device to set up a session for an endpoint.

messages.label: NCA (DIAMETER_SUCCESS)
messages.note: Sent after session state is created, only if the device can comply.

messages.label: NCR (UPDATE_REQUEST)
messages.note: Changes the behavior of an existing session.

messages.label: Accounting stop
messages.note: Reports all session bindings; the device MAY send it.

messages.label: STA (DIAMETER_SUCCESS)
messages.note: Sent after the bindings and session state are removed.

items.label: INITIAL_REQUEST
items.desc: Starts a NAT control session between the peers.

items.label: UPDATE_REQUEST
items.desc: Updates, adds or removes bindings on an access session.

items.label: QUERY_REQUEST
items.desc: Asks the NAT device about currently installed bindings for an endpoint.
